* Once I’m finished putting everything together for the day I turn the music off and begin my “commute”

a blog called “The Pragmatic Christian” (and I was going through the various iterations of ideas as I was deciding the name for the blog), I began by thinking about William James.

In his book Pragmatism, James describes the “cash value” of an idea or theory. In other words, he thought about ideas in terms of how they worked in actual life or in real situations.

But I got thinking… I realized that there had to be a way for someone to use pragmatism to defend a religious belief or worldview—that someone should be able to prove the existence of God or that Christianity was true using James’ “cash value” as the litmus test. I decided that I would give this a try.

Well, when I started this idea of a blog, the first thing I had to do was decide how I would define “pragmatism.” Here is the definition that I came up with: “If I believe that the truth or value of an idea is found by looking at its effects in real life, then I am a pragmatic person.”

From that definition, it became easier to put together a definition for the name I had chosen for my blog. I realized that by defining “pragmatism” I had defined “the pragmatic Christian.” I figured out that, if I wanted to use the definition of pragmatism that I had laid out earlier, “the pragmatic Christian” would be someone who believed that “God exists because of its effects in real life.”

So, that’s where we are today. I have an idea that God exists and that Christianity is true—but my reason for believing that is that I have experienced these effects in real life. I have seen how believing in God has helped me with different things in my life. I have seen how it has helped my friends and family. And I have seen how it has brought people closer together.

raw_response.text:
schedule and started my work. I’d planned to have the rough draft in around six weeks, but then something happened: I found myself staring blankly at my keyboard.

The problem was that what I was doing didn’t feel like a manuscript.

The title was there, the characters were there, and I’d begun setting up the plot, but I’d forgotten something important. I didn’t know what my characters wanted, and because of this, everything else fell apart.

It’s easy to think of character development as a way to make your characters three-dimensional. And when a character is three-dimensional, it follows that the person is “real” and that the reader will believe in them. The problem is, in a world of flat, two-dimensional cardboard cut-outs—even if the writing is amazing—it’s the character who is going to keep the reader’s interest.

When I began my first round of rewrites, I found that the most interesting and powerful character was the one with the biggest want.

The biggest want for her was to get through the day without having to give up her dreams—to be something other than the girl with the mental illness. In doing so, however, I found her most desperate fear: that she would end up like her mom. And that fear became the root of every story choice she made.

The problem with her was not that she was un-relatable—she was so relatable I could’ve gotten lost in her story. The problem was that her story was not interesting—it wasn’t until her character’s wants were more complicated than just “to get through the day” that I could create a meaningful narrative.

, as I watch people act selfishly and carelessly and I wonder, Is this the best of us?

I’m afraid that the answer, at least for now, is no.

It feels like my faith is being tested and it’s tempting to jump ship. I even went on Facebook recently to post my resignation, explaining how disappointed I’ve been in the human race, and then I thought, well, let me just do some reading and maybe some research, because maybe there’s something I’m not seeing that’s different.

There are plenty of stories of people being kind and loving and generous and all those things. But when I search for them, I don’t see them in the news cycle. I’m not just talking about my country, though. What’s playing out in the U.S. is happening on other shores, too.

The hoarding. The panic. The blaming.

Yes, some of the fear is rooted in the unknown. Yes, it’s a time to take precautions. Yes, some of the uncertainty may have been overblown. And yes, it’s natural for people to try to prepare for the worst. But the collective behaviour I’m seeing — even in my own country, which has always been one of the wealthiest in the world — makes it seem like everyone’s in survival mode.

It seems like I’m asking people to do more, when they might just want to be selfish and secure their own fate.

It’s hard to imagine that people would take to social media to make fun of others if we were really living in a time of community and solidarity. But that’s the reality, not just in my Facebook feed, but in feeds around the world.
